items.prompt: In marketing copy, what does the abbreviation CTA stand for?

options.label: Content target audience
Click-through average
Customer trust assurance
Call to action

rubric: CTA means call to action, the prompt telling the reader what to do next.
Other options are invented expansions of the acronym.

items.prompt: Which of these statements is a benefit rather than a feature?

options.label: Made from recycled aluminium
Never run out of space for your holiday photos
Has a 5000 mAh battery
Includes 256GB of storage

rubric: A benefit states what the product does for the reader; the key describes the outcome.
The other options describe product specifications, which are features.

items.prompt: What is the main job of a headline in an ad or on a landing page?

options.label: To explain the whole pricing structure
To grab attention and make the reader keep reading
To give the company's full legal name
To list every product feature in one line

rubric: A headline's first job is to earn attention and pull the reader into the body copy.
Other options describe details that belong in the body or footer.

items.prompt: In the AIDA copywriting model, what do the four letters stand for?

options.label: Audience, Intent, Data, Analysis
Appeal, Impact, Discount, Advert
Attention, Interest, Desire, Action
Awareness, Insight, Demand, Approval

rubric: AIDA stands for Attention, Interest, Desire, Action.
Other options are plausible-sounding but incorrect word sets.

items.prompt: What is a 'lead magnet' in email marketing copy?

options.label: A banner that stays fixed at the top of a page
A discount shown only on the checkout page
A subject line written in capital letters
A free resource offered in exchange for a reader's email address

rubric: A lead magnet is a free guide, checklist or similar item offered for contact details.
Other options are unrelated tactics or layout features.

items.prompt: Which of the following are common elements of persuasive landing page copy? Select all that apply.

options.label: Call to action
Internal cost spreadsheet
Headline
Server error log
Customer testimonial

rubric: Headlines, calls to action and testimonials are standard landing page elements.
Cost spreadsheets and error logs are internal documents, not reader-facing copy.

items.prompt: Maya is writing a promotional email for a bakery. She knows readers see the sender name and one line of text in their inbox before deciding whether to open it. Which part of the email is that line of text called?

options.label: The signature
The unsubscribe link
The footer
The subject line

rubric: The subject line is what readers see in the inbox and it drives opens.
Signature, footer and unsubscribe link only appear after the email is opened.

items.prompt: Why do copywriters usually lead with benefits instead of features?

options.label: Benefits are always shorter than feature lists
Readers already know every feature before they see an ad
Features are legally not allowed in ads
Readers mostly want to know what the product will do for them

rubric: Readers act when they see how the product improves their situation.
Distractors give false reasons: legal bans, length, or assumed prior knowledge.

items.prompt: A product page says 'Only 3 left in stock.' Which persuasion technique is this line using?

options.label: Price anchoring
Social proof
Scarcity and urgency
Storytelling

rubric: Limited availability prompts faster action, which is scarcity and urgency.
Social proof relies on others' approval; anchoring compares prices.

items.prompt: Why is the headline 'Lose 5 kg in 8 weeks' usually stronger than 'Lose weight fast'?

options.label: Because numbers are required in all headlines
Because longer headlines always rank higher
Because a specific, concrete claim is more believable and easier to picture
Because it avoids mentioning the reader's goal

rubric: Specific claims feel credible and tangible to readers.
Distractors state false rules or misread the headline's content.

items.prompt: What does a customer review on a product page do for persuasion?

options.label: It makes the call to action unnecessary
It explains how the product was manufactured
It shows people like the reader trusted the product and were satisfied
It replaces the need for a price

rubric: Reviews act as social proof, reducing the reader's perceived risk.
Other options give functions that reviews do not perform.

items.prompt: Why do most email copywriting guides recommend one main call to action per email?

options.label: Readers dislike clicking any button at all
Two calls to action cost twice as much to send
Email software blocks messages with more than one link
A single clear action keeps readers focused instead of making them choose

rubric: One clear next step reduces decision friction and raises response.
Distractors invent technical or cost limits.

items.prompt: Which of these lines are written in a benefit-led way for a mattress ad? Select all that apply.

options.label: Layered with 5 cm of memory foam
Wake up without back pain
Contains 1,200 pocket springs
Fall asleep faster every night

rubric: The first two lines state outcomes for the sleeper, so they are benefits.
Springs and foam depth are features that describe the product itself.

items.prompt: Leo is writing a landing page for scheduling software aimed at busy small-business owners. His draft opens with three paragraphs on the company's founding history. A mentor tells him to change the opening for this audience. Which change fits her advice best?

options.label: Move the founders' photos above the history to add a personal touch
Open with how much admin time owners save, since they are short on time
Add a longer history so owners trust the company's age
Replace the history with technical details of the code behind the software

rubric: Busy owners respond to a quick, relevant benefit such as time saved.
Other options keep the focus on the company or on technical detail rather than the reader's goal.

items.prompt: Which line states a benefit rather than only a feature?

options.label: Available in four colours and two screen sizes
Charge once and stream all week away from any socket
Packed with a 5000 mAh battery and fast charging
Built around a fast octa-core processor chip

rubric: A benefit says what the product does for the reader's life; the key describes the outcome of the battery.
The other options list specifications or options, which are features.

items.prompt: Why does a button reading 'Get my free guide' usually work better than one reading 'Submit'?

options.label: It lets the brand name appear more often on the page for recall
It makes the button longer, and longer buttons always get more clicks
It tells readers exactly what they get by clicking, reducing uncertainty
It avoids using a verb, so readers feel no pressure to commit

rubric: Specific, reader-focused CTAs state the payoff of acting, which lowers hesitation.
Distractors rely on length or branding, which are not why specific CTAs convert.

items.prompt: What is the main job of a headline in an ad or on a landing page?

options.label: Win attention and promise something relevant so the reader keeps reading
Show the brand's history so readers trust the company before reading on
Summarise every feature so readers need not read the body copy
Spell out price and terms in full detail before anything else appears

rubric: A headline earns the next sentence by being relevant and promising value.
Other options overload the headline with details that belong in the body.

items.prompt: 'Only 3 seats left at this price' is mainly an example of which persuasion technique?

options.label: Authority
Scarcity
Storytelling
Social proof

rubric: Limited availability signals scarcity, which prompts quicker action.
Social proof and authority rely on others' behaviour or expertise, which this line lacks.

items.prompt: Why does 'You'll finish reports in half the time' usually beat 'Our software finishes reports faster'?

options.label: It hides the product so curiosity forces readers to click through
It avoids making any promise, so readers cannot disagree with it
It uses fewer syllables, which readers find easier to trust
It centres the reader's own outcome instead of the company's claim

rubric: Reader-centred wording lets people picture their own result.
Distractors misattribute the effect to word length, mystery or lack of a promise.

items.prompt: Which of these lines work as social proof? Select all that apply.

options.label: Our founder has always had a passion for design
Offer ends at midnight tonight
Used by teams at three well-known banks
Rated 4.8 by more than 12,000 customers
Free shipping on all orders over 50 dollars

rubric: Social proof shows that other people have used and approved the product.
The founder line, shipping offer and deadline are brand story, incentive and urgency instead.

items.prompt: A fitness brand emails people who have never heard of its app and don't realise they have a posture problem. The draft opens: 'Our app has 40 exercise modules and AI tracking.' What is the most likely result?

options.label: Readers click because a long feature list creates a sense of urgency
Readers skip it because it opens with the product, not a problem they recognise
Readers respond well because detailed features prove credibility to unaware audiences
Readers convert because cold audiences prefer technical specs over a relatable hook

rubric: Readers unaware of a problem need a recognisable problem or benefit first, not product features.
Distractors assume features alone create interest or urgency in a cold audience.

items.prompt: A phone is waterproof to 10 metres and aimed at holiday-makers. Which line best turns this feature into a benefit?

options.label: Our waterproof design uses premium sealed ports and strong glass
Rated IP68 and sealed with gaskets around every single port
Tested to a depth of 10 metres in our lab for thirty minutes
Film the dive, the pool party and the surprise storm without worry

rubric: The key shows what the audience can now do and feel because of the feature.
The others restate the waterproofing in technical or testing terms.

items.prompt: A first-time visitor to a blog sees a form to join the email list. Which button text best fits this low-commitment goal?

options.label: Download the annual contract
Send me the weekly tips
Book a 60-minute consultation
Buy the full course now

rubric: Cold visitors need a small, clear, benefit-focused step.
The other CTAs ask for money, time or paperwork too early.

items.prompt: A meal-kit company wants busy parents to sign up. Which headline is best for that audience and goal?

options.label: Introducing the most innovative meal kit platform on the market
Dinner on the table in 20 minutes, with no planning or shopping
Our chefs trained in Michelin kitchens across Europe and Asia
Meal kits: a brief history of home cooking and convenience

rubric: It speaks to the parents' main pain, time, with a concrete outcome.
The others are brand-centred, prestige-focused or off-topic.

items.prompt: You are using the Problem-Agitate-Solve formula. You've written: 'Your emails go unread and sales stall.' What should come next?

options.label: Agitate by showing what staying stuck will cost the reader
Add a customer testimonial and a star rating
Close with a countdown deadline and a button
Offer the product at once and state its price

rubric: After stating the problem, PAS deepens the felt consequences before the solution.
Other options skip the agitation step and jump ahead.

items.prompt: A webinar sign-up page has buttons for 'Register', 'Read our blog', 'Follow us' and 'Download brochure', and few people register. Which change best applies the one-goal principle?

options.label: Move the registration button to the footer for a cleaner look
Replace the buttons with a long paragraph explaining every option
Add more buttons so every reader finds a favourite action
Remove competing links and repeat one 'Save my seat' button

rubric: A landing page converts best when it focuses on a single action.
Adding options or hiding the CTA dilutes or buries the goal.

items.prompt: A language-app ad reads: 'Learn Spanish with our app. Many features. Click here.' Which edits would improve it for beginners wanting to travel? Select all that apply.

options.label: Replace 'Many features' with 'Hold a basic café chat in 4 weeks'
Open with a long history of the Spanish language
Change 'Click here' to 'Start my first lesson free'
Add the company's founding year and office locations
Add adjectives such as amazing and revolutionary

rubric: A specific CTA and a concrete benefit for the traveller audience apply benefit-led copy.
Vague adjectives and company or language history don't serve the reader's goal.

items.prompt: A handmade-candle product page has the add-to-cart button above the fold, but customer reviews sit in a tab at the bottom. Visitors view the page but hesitate to buy. Which change best applies proof to this problem?

options.label: Show a pop-up asking for an email before the page can be viewed
Put a short customer quote with its star rating beside the add-to-cart button
Replace the reviews with a longer story about the brand's founding
Move the price to the footer so it doesn't scare visitors

rubric: Proof placed next to the action answers doubt at the moment of decision.
The other changes hide information, add friction or swap proof for brand story.

items.prompt: A note-taking app's feature is "syncs across devices in real time." You are writing a headline for busy freelancers who switch between phone and laptop. Which headline turns the feature into a benefit for them?

options.label: Sync, sync and sync again with our powerful and flexible new app
Introducing the smartest sync engine on the market for modern teams
Real-time cross-device sync technology is built into every single plan
Start a task on your phone, finish it on your laptop, lose nothing

rubric: The key shows what the freelancer can now do, which is the benefit.
Distractors restate the feature or use empty hype instead of an outcome.

items.prompt: You are writing the button text for an email that offers a free 14-day trial of invoicing software. The goal is trial sign-ups from readers wary of commitment. Which call to action fits best?

options.label: Submit your details to our sales department for follow-up today
Click here to read more about our company and its history
Buy the annual plan now before our prices go up next month
Start my free 14-day trial, no card needed

rubric: The key is action-specific and lowers the perceived risk for wary readers.
Distractors are vague, off-goal, or ask for a bigger commitment than the reader is ready for.

items.prompt: You are structuring a landing page with the AIDA model (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action). The headline has captured Attention. What should the copy that follows it do?

options.label: Place the purchase button immediately so no momentum is lost after the headline
Present a countdown discount to create desire before the reader knows the product
Expand on the reader's problem with a relevant detail that keeps them reading
Add legal disclaimers and terms so the reader trusts the offer first

rubric: After Attention comes Interest: a relevant detail that sustains reading.
Distractors jump ahead to Desire or Action, or insert material that is not a stage of AIDA.

items.prompt: A bakery has 12 seats left in its Saturday sourdough class and is emailing past customers. Which subject line applies specificity and honest urgency best?

options.label: Newsletter: April updates and news from Hearth Bakery team
12 seats left: Saturday sourdough class at 10am
Last chance ever to learn how to bake absolutely anything
Don't miss out on our amazing baking classes this season!!!

rubric: The key gives concrete detail and a true scarcity cue.
Distractors are vague, exaggerated or purely informational with no reason to open.

items.prompt: A draft reads: "We are proud to offer a scheduling platform that our team built for managers." You are asked to make it reader-focused. Which rewrite does that best?

options.label: Plan your team's whole week in ten minutes instead of an hour
Our talented team is proud to have built this scheduling platform
We built a scheduling platform because managers asked us for one
Managers are the main users of our proud new scheduling platform

rubric: The key speaks to "you" and states an outcome.
Distractors keep the company as the subject or only change the wording around the same self-focused claim.

items.prompt: A headphone brand lists features and wants copy that states a benefit to the reader. Which of these lines do that? Select all that apply.

options.label: Leave the charger at home for a whole week of commuting
Our brand is proud of its award-winning audio heritage
Take them out in the rain without worrying about damage
Powered by an industry-leading 30-hour battery cell design
Engineered with a 10mm dynamic driver and titanium coating

rubric: Lines 0 and 2 describe what the reader gets to do or avoid.
The others restate specs or company pride without a reader outcome.

items.prompt: You are writing the landing page headline for a meal-kit service. The audience is new parents who are short on time and sleep. The only goal is first-box sign-ups. Which headline best applies that audience and goal?

options.label: Dinner on the table in 20 minutes, even after a sleepless night
Meal kits are changing how the whole country eats dinner tonight
Fresh seasonal ingredients sourced from small local farms near you
Sign up today and get 40% off your very first delivery box

rubric: The key targets the audience's specific pain: time and exhaustion.
Distractors are generic, about the company's trend, or lead with a discount that ignores the audience.

items.prompt: A promotional email has a 40% open rate but a 0.5% click rate. The subject line promised "a free guide to cutting your ad costs," while the body opens with company news and the button reads "Learn more." What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The body and button don't deliver the subject line's promise of a free guide
The subject line is too weak to earn attention from this list
The list is too small for either rate to mean anything at all
The send time is wrong, so readers skip the message after opening it

rubric: High opens show the subject worked; the drop-off points to a mismatch between promise and body or CTA.
Distractors blame the subject, list size or timing, which the open rate does not support.

items.prompt: In an A/B test, version B changed the landing page headline and also switched the button from grey to orange. B converted 20% better. A colleague says the new headline is proven. What is the flaw in that conclusion?

options.label: Headlines can only be judged by open rates, not by conversion rates
A 20% lift is too large to be believable in any headline test
Two things changed, so the lift can't be attributed to the headline alone
Orange buttons always convert better, so the headline had no effect at all

rubric: Changing two variables confounds the result.
Distractors replace the confound with a blanket rule, a disbelief of size, or a wrong metric claim.

items.prompt: Two ads target a cold audience who have never heard of a budgeting app. Ad 1 says "Save 20% on your first year." Ad 2 says "Still wondering where your pay goes each month?" Ad 2 gets far more sign-ups. Which analysis best explains this?

options.label: Problem-led copy suits readers unaware of a need, while a discount assumes interest
Questions always outperform offers because readers like to be asked things
The discount was too small, and a 40% discount would have won easily
Ad 1 failed because it mentions the price, which should never appear in ads

rubric: Awareness level determines which message works; a discount presumes existing interest.
Distractors offer universal rules or a pricing explanation that ignores the audience's awareness.

items.prompt: A page says: "Revolutionary, best-in-class, world-class solutions for every business need. Contact us." Visitors leave without enquiring. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: Vague superlatives with no proof or specific outcome make the claims hard to believe
Using the word "contact" is too pushy for a business audience to accept
The copy is too specific, which narrows the audience who might respond
The page is too short, and adding three more paragraphs would fix it

rubric: Unsupported superlatives lack credibility and give no concrete reason to act.
Distractors blame length, the CTA wording, or specificity, which is the opposite of the real problem.

items.prompt: A product page for a single backpack has the buttons "Buy now," "Join our newsletter," "Follow us on Instagram" and "Read our blog," all the same size. Purchases are low. What is the most likely problem?

options.label: Newsletter sign-ups always reduce purchases by lowering buyer trust
The buy button is too visible and scares off shoppers who are unsure
The page lacks enough links, so shoppers can't explore the brand properly
Competing calls to action split attention away from the one goal of purchase

rubric: Multiple equal CTAs dilute focus on the page's single goal.
Distractors misread visibility, propose more links, or state an unfounded absolute.

items.prompt: A product page shows this testimonial: "Great product! Highly recommend. – J." Which flaws weaken it as proof? Select all that apply.

options.label: It says nothing specific about the problem solved or result
It gives no full name or role, so it can't be verified
It appears on the product page rather than the homepage
It is written in the first person, which hurts credibility

rubric: Unverifiable source and lack of specifics both weaken proof.
First-person voice is normal for testimonials, and page placement isn't a credibility flaw.

items.prompt: A software firm sends a welcome series to people who just downloaded a free checklist. Email 1 delivers the checklist. Email 2, sent the next day, pushes the annual plan with a 30% discount, and 60% of recipients unsubscribe. What best explains the unsubscribes?

options.label: The discount was too small to interest anyone who had just joined the list
Sending an email one day after sign-up is too soon for any message at all
Email 2 asks for a purchase before value and trust have been built with new subscribers
The checklist topic was probably wrong for the whole audience that downloaded it

rubric: Early hard selling mismatches the subscribers' stage of trust.
Distractors blame the discount size, topic or timing, which do not account for the sharp drop at the sales email.

items.prompt: An ad says "Stop missing deadlines." It lands on a page headed "Powerful Work Management Platform." Click-through is strong but most visitors leave within seconds. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The headline is too short to carry search keywords, so visitors cannot tell what the product does
The ad's wording is too negative, so visitors distrust the brand before they reach the page content
The ad reaches too broad an audience, so most of the clicks come from people who will never buy
The headline does not echo the ad's promise, so visitors cannot confirm they are in the right place

rubric: Message match: the page must continue the promise that earned the click, or visitors doubt they are in the right place.
Distractors blame tone, keywords or targeting, which would not explain strong clicks followed by instant exits.

items.prompt: Two subject lines go to equal halves of a list. A: "Your 20% discount ends tonight" gets 28% opens and 1.1% purchases. B: "How Maria cut her prep time in half" gets 19% opens and 1.9% purchases. Which analysis is best?

options.label: A mainly drew discount-driven readers with weak interest in the product, while B drew readers who want the outcome
B won because a first name raises trust, so any subject line featuring a person would beat A reliably
B is the better line, because open rate is the main measure of subject-line quality and A already won on it
A failed because urgency never works in email, so the deadline wording alone explains the purchase gap

rubric: Opens measure curiosity; purchases show who the line attracted, and discount framing can pull in low-intent readers.
Distractors over-trust open rate, overgeneralise about urgency, or credit names without evidence.

items.prompt: A phone page for buyers over 65 reads: "6.7-inch AMOLED, 120Hz, 5000mAh, IP68." Sales are low and many buyers phone to ask what the terms mean. What is the main flaw?

options.label: Too few specs are listed, so buyers who compare models lack enough numbers to trust the product
The page has no urgency language, so buyers who understand the specs still delay the purchase decision
The specs are not translated into outcomes this audience values, such as readable text and all-day use
Numbers weaken persuasion on any product page, so the specs should give way to adjectives like "premium"

rubric: Features need translating into benefits the specific audience cares about; jargon leaves them unable to see the value.
Distractors suggest more specs, no numbers, or urgency, none of which fix the comprehension gap.

items.prompt: With a large enough sample, a landing page variant that changes the headline, hero image and button colour together lifts sign-ups by 18%. What can the team soundly conclude?

options.label: The button colour caused the lift, because it is the last element a reader sees before they act
The headline caused the lift, because headline changes usually have the largest effect on sign-ups
The variant as a whole beat the original, but they cannot tell which change produced the gain
Nothing can be concluded, because any test showing an 18% lift is too large to be a real effect

rubric: Changing several elements at once confounds the test, so only the bundle can be credited.
Distractors attribute the lift to one element by assumption or dismiss a valid result.

items.prompt: A $1,997 course is sold to cold social-media traffic with a 150-word page and one button. Visitors read it but rarely buy. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: Short copy always reads as lazy, so the price would be accepted if the page simply had more paragraphs
The button is too prominent, so cold visitors feel pushed before they have looked at the page
A high-priced, high-commitment offer to unfamiliar visitors needs space for proof, detail and objection handling
The page is missing a countdown timer, which is the main driver of purchases at every price point

rubric: Cost and commitment rise with price, and cold readers need trust-building and answers to objections before acting.
Distractors blame button prominence, a timer or length for its own sake rather than the missing persuasive content.

items.prompt: A serum ad reads: "The world's best, revolutionary skincare serum. Dermatologists love it. Results guaranteed!" Which parts weaken its credibility? Select all that apply.

options.label: The sentences are short, which makes the copy read as rushed and unprofessional
Naming the product as a "skincare serum" limits appeal to too narrow a segment
"Dermatologists love it" gives vague social proof with no named source or figure
"World's best" is an unsupported superlative with no evidence behind it
"Results guaranteed!" promises an outcome with no terms or timeframe stated

rubric: Unsupported superlatives, vague proof and unqualified guarantees all invite scepticism.
Short sentences and a clear product category are normal strengths in persuasive copy.

items.prompt: A SaaS company's day-3 trial email gets a 42% open rate but a 1% click rate. The body has a welcome note, a blog link, a webinar link, an upgrade link and a "Reply with questions" line. Which cause is most likely?

options.label: Links inside body copy are penalised by inbox filters, so readers never see the clickable text
The subject line is weak, since a 42% open rate shows readers did not find the email appealing
The email is too short to build trust, since click rates rise only once an email passes 500 words
Several competing calls to action split attention, so no single next step is clear to the reader

rubric: Strong opens with weak clicks point to the body; multiple CTAs dilute the one action wanted.
Distractors misread the open rate, invent a word-count rule, or blame filters.

items.prompt: An invoicing tool for freelancers needs a landing-page headline for cold traffic. Criteria: state a specific outcome, avoid hype, and make sense without context. Which headline best meets all three?

options.label: Get paid in 7 days, not 30: invoicing built for freelancers
The world's smartest invoicing revolution for every freelancer
Meet Ledgerly: where freelancing and finance come together
Finally, a better way to work with money and your clients

rubric: It names a concrete, checkable outcome in plain language and identifies the audience.
Distractors are hype, vague, or brand-led with no outcome.

items.prompt: A page offers a 14-day free trial with no card required. Criteria: match the low commitment, say what the reader gets, and reduce friction. Which button text is best?

options.label: Click here to find out more about the product
Start my free 14-day trial, no card needed
Get started with our premium plan right away
Sign up today and don't miss out on our offer

rubric: It states the specific offer and removes the main fear (card details), fitting the low-commitment goal.
Distractors are vague, push a paid commitment, or send readers away from the action.

items.prompt: Judging a supplement ad for credibility and compliance risk, which claim is the riskiest?

options.label: "Made with 12 plant extracts", a factual ingredient count that can easily be checked
"Clinically proven to cure arthritis", which implies a disease cure that would need rigorous evidence
"Our customers say they feel more energetic", a soft claim based on reported feelings
"Try it for 30 days or your money back", a refund offer with clear terms to follow

rubric: Disease-cure claims need strong evidence and are the most likely to draw regulatory and credibility trouble.
The other claims are soft, verifiable or offer-based, so they carry less risk.

items.prompt: A course seller wants launch urgency. Criteria: protect long-term trust, keep repeat buyers, and still lift conversions. Which approach fits best?

options.label: Use a countdown timer that resets for each visitor, since it creates urgency on every visit
Quietly extend the deadline whenever sales are slow, so the offer stays live for every visitor
Close enrolment on a real date tied to the cohort start, state why, then honour it
Say "only 3 spots left" on every page whether or not capacity is limited, to keep pressure on

rubric: A real, explained deadline creates urgency without damaging trust when honoured.
Fake timers, shifting deadlines and invented scarcity erode credibility once noticed.

items.prompt: A colleague rewrites "Cut invoice chasing from 6 hours to 1 a week" as "Transform your finance workflow." Judged on believability and clarity, which critique is best?

options.label: The rewrite is better because shorter, broader phrases appeal to more segments and so raise conversions
The rewrite is weaker because it removes a specific, checkable outcome and replaces it with an abstract claim
The rewrite is better because verbs like "transform" are proven to trigger action more than numbers do
The rewrite is weaker only because the original used digits, which are always more persuasive than words

rubric: Specific, concrete outcomes are more believable and easier to picture than abstract claims.
Distractors defend vagueness as broad appeal or reduce the issue to digits versus words.

items.prompt: Which are sound reasons to choose a short-form page over a long-form one? Select all that apply.

options.label: The audience is warm and already knows the brand and the offer
Shorter copy always ranks higher because page length alone sets search position
The product is a low-priced impulse purchase with few objections to answer
Few questions or doubts stand between the reader and the decision
Short copy always outperforms because people do not read online

rubric: Short pages suit low-commitment, familiar offers with few objections to handle.
Absolute claims about reading habits or rankings ignore the offer and audience.

items.prompt: A B2B accounting tool targets small-business owners with cold LinkedIn ads. The goal is demo bookings. Criteria: name a pain they recognise, give one clear action, and ask for low commitment. Which draft best meets them?

options.label: "Our founder started this company after a tax audit went wrong. Read the full story on our blog."
"Month-end eating your weekend? See it close in 15 minutes. Book a 15-minute demo."
"Accounting, reimagined. The trusted name in modern business finance. Learn more at our website today."
"Invoicing, payroll, tax, reporting, budgets and 7 more features. Compare plans, download the guide, or call us."

rubric: It names a familiar pain, offers one low-commitment action, and fits the demo goal.
Distractors tell a story with no ask, scatter several CTAs, or rely on empty brand slogans.

items.prompt: Two subject lines are tested. Variant A: 20% open rate, 5% of openers click. Variant B: 28% open rate, 3% of openers click. The landing page and purchase rate are identical. The goal is sales per email sent. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Ship B: opens are the earliest funnel step, so the gain compounds into more sales later
Either: the open-rate gain and click-rate loss cancel out, so choose on brand tone
Ship A: it earns 1.0 clicks per 100 sends against 0.84 for B
Ship B: the higher open rate shows its subject line persuades more people to engage

rubric: Sales per send depends on open rate times click rate: 0.20x0.05=1.0% vs 0.28x0.03=0.84%.
Distractors reward opens as a vanity metric or assume the trade-off is neutral.

items.prompt: Cold, problem-unaware social traffic sees this ad headline: 'Introducing FlowSync 3.0: AI-powered two-way calendar sync.' Judged against the audience's awareness level, which critique is strongest?

options.label: It is sound, because naming the version and the AI technology builds authority with readers who don't know the brand
It opens with the product and its features, but readers don't yet feel the problem, so lead with a situation they recognise
It lacks a superlative, and claiming 'the best' would give unaware readers the credibility to keep reading
It is too short, because cold audiences need 20+ words to grasp what the technology does and why it matters

rubric: Problem-unaware readers respond to a recognised problem or outcome, not a product announcement.
Distractors rely on length, superlatives or authority cues that don't address awareness.

items.prompt: A skincare brand has only a self-reported survey: 87% of 52 users said their skin looked smoother after 4 weeks. There is no clinical trial. Criteria: persuasive, truthful and defensible if challenged. Which line is best?

options.label: Clinically proven to smooth skin in 4 weeks
Most users get visibly smoother skin, guaranteed in 4 weeks
Dermatologists agree: smoother skin in just 4 weeks
87% of 52 testers said their skin looked smoother after 4 weeks

rubric: It states a specific, accurately scoped result with sample size, so it is persuasive and defensible.
Others imply clinical or expert backing or a guarantee the evidence does not support.

items.prompt: Cold search traffic is landing on a page for software with a $24,000/year contract bought by a committee. The criterion is lead quality over lead volume. Which page approach is best?

options.label: Short page with a countdown offer, since urgency makes up for the missing trust that cold traffic brings with it
Long page answering committee objections with proof, since high-risk purchases need evidence before anyone books contact
Short page with one headline and a demo button, since fewer words reduce friction for every audience and deal size
Long page of feature lists, since committees compare specifications first and consider outcomes or risk much later

rubric: High-commitment, multi-stakeholder, cold-traffic offers need proof and objection handling to qualify leads.
Short-page and urgency options optimise volume, not quality; feature lists ignore risk and outcomes.

items.prompt: A brand emails the same list monthly. The criterion is long-term trust and repeat sales, not just today's conversion. Which urgency tactic is best?

options.label: Daily 'last chance' emails in the final week, since repetition guarantees every subscriber notices the deadline before it passes
A real cohort deadline with the date and reason stated, since readers can verify it and will believe the next offer too
An evergreen countdown timer that resets on every visit, since it creates a sense of urgency for every reader who arrives
'Only 3 left' on every product page, since scarcity wording lifts conversion whether or not the stock level is accurate

rubric: A verifiable deadline keeps urgency credible, protecting trust across repeat sends.
Fake timers, false scarcity and over-sending win short-term clicks but erode trust.

items.prompt: A team rewrites 'We help businesses grow' as 'Cut invoice chasing from 6 hours to 1 a week.' Which are valid reasons the rewrite is stronger? Select all that apply.

options.label: A specific outcome lets readers quickly self-qualify
It names a pain the right reader recognises, improving relevance
A concrete claim is more believable and can be backed with proof
Shorter headlines always outperform longer ones
Numbers raise conversion regardless of whether readers believe them

rubric: Specificity aids self-qualification, credibility and relevance.
Distractors overgeneralise: numbers only help if believable, and length is not a universal rule.

items.prompt: A paid social ad promises a 'Free budget template'. The landing page headline reads 'Book a demo of FinPlan', and 85% of visitors leave within 10 seconds. The demo must remain the end goal. Which change is best?

options.label: Add three customer logos and a security badge above the demo form to raise credibility quickly
Match the headline to the template, gate the file by email, then invite engaged readers to a demo
Add a countdown timer to the demo offer so that visitors decide before they think of leaving
Cut the demo form to one field so that more of the visitors submit before they decide to leave

rubric: The core problem is message mismatch; fulfilling the ad's promise keeps the demo as a later step.
Other options add trust, urgency or less friction to an offer visitors never wanted.

items.prompt: Write a headline for an insulated bottle aimed at commuters. Constraints: at most 9 words, states the reader's outcome, contains a concrete number, makes no unprovable superlative. Which meets all four?

options.label: Ice still frozen after 12 hours in your bag
Premium stainless steel keeps your drinks colder for longer
The world's best bottle keeps drinks cold for 12 hours
Built from 18/8 stainless steel for your daily commute

rubric: It states an outcome, includes a number, uses 9 words and has no superlative.
Distractors break one constraint each: superlative and length, no number, or feature not outcome.

items.prompt: Design a 3-email abandoned-cart sequence for a $300 chair. Constraints: no discount in email 1, address the main objection (returns), and escalate the incentive only at the end. Which sequence fits?

options.label: 1: reminder plus reviews; 2: 30-day returns and setup guide; 3: free-shipping offer with deadline
1: 15% code with cart photo; 2: reviews roundup for social proof; 3: returns policy link and expiry notice
1: brand story and values; 2: 20% code to restart interest; 3: urgent expiry notice with cart photo
1: reminder with cart photo; 2: same reminder reworded; 3: expiry notice with a 20% discount code

rubric: It meets all constraints: no early discount, objection handled in the middle, incentive last.
Distractors discount early, skip the returns objection, or lead with discounts.

items.prompt: Choose the button text for a free-trial page aimed at wary accountants. Constraints: first-person voice, says what the click delivers, and removes payment risk. Which meets all three?

options.label: Join thousands of accountants now
Get started with FirmFlow today
Create my free account, no card needed
Submit my details to continue

rubric: It is first-person, names the deliverable and removes payment risk.
Distractors are generic, form-like, or lean on social proof without addressing risk.

items.prompt: A landing page has a 9-field form. 62% of visitors scroll to it, but 4% complete it. Sales needs company size and phone before the first call, though these can be collected after sign-up. Which redesign fits?

options.label: Move the form to the footer with a long FAQ above it so only committed visitors reach the form
Ask for email first, then collect company size and phone on a second step once the lead is captured
Remove company size and phone permanently so sales can qualify every lead from the email address alone
Keep all nine fields but add a headline stressing how quickly visitors can fill in the whole form

rubric: A two-step form cuts initial friction while still gathering the fields sales requires.
Distractors drop required data, ignore friction, or reduce completions by hiding the form.

items.prompt: Write a line for a herbal sleep supplement. Constraints: no claim to treat or cure a condition, no unsupported proof claim, and still benefit-led. Which meets all three?

options.label: Cures restless nights with a clinically formulated herbal blend, made to help you sleep soundly again
Guaranteed deep sleep tonight or your money back, a blend that doctors approve for people who struggle to rest
Finally treat insomnia naturally with chamomile and lemon balm, a gentle alternative to prescription sleep aids
Wind down tonight with a calming blend of chamomile and lemon balm, made for an easier evening routine

rubric: It promises a modest, evening-routine benefit with no disease or proof claim.
Distractors make cure, treatment or doctor-approval claims, or a guarantee that cannot be supported.

items.prompt: You plan an A/B test of two headlines. The plan must give a result attributable to the headline, avoid false winners, and tie to revenue. Which elements belong in it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Also change the image and button so the best combination wins
Set purchases per visitor as the primary metric before launch
Stop on the first day the dashboard shows 95% confidence
Change only the headline between variants
Fix the sample size and run length before launching

rubric: A single changed variable, a pre-set sample and a revenue metric meet the three constraints.
Early stopping inflates false positives; multi-change tests lose attribution.

items.prompt: A $300 ergonomic chair page has strong traffic. Reviews show buyers fear difficult assembly and awkward returns. Constraints: one opening paragraph, lead with a benefit, defuse both fears, make no unprovable claims. Which opening fits?

options.label: Order today for a limited-time $40 discount while stocks last and save on premium seating built to give years of use.
The world's most comfortable chair, loved by thousands of owners, so you will never regret the purchase or want to return it.
Engineered with 14 adjustment points, 4D arms and breathable mesh to suit every body type and every working posture you use.
Back pain after long workdays? Sit comfortably from day one: 20-minute assembly with one tool, 60-day free returns.

rubric: It leads with a benefit and addresses both assembly and returns with checkable specifics.
Distractors use unprovable superlatives, lead with features, or use discounts and ignore the fears.
